input.question: Diploid vs Haploid cells
input.ground_truth: Cells start as diploid (two copies of each chromosome). They replicate their DNA in S-phase and become tetraploid (4 copies of each chromosome). After mitosis that number is divided by two so each daughter cell is diploid (two copies). In meiosis another division reduces the ploidy so you get four haploid (one copy) gametes. This is in us and many other organisms. The model organism [*Xenopus laevis*](_URL_0_) is tetraploid (four copies of each chromosome). Some plants have [very high ploidy](_URL_1_).

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Diploid vs Haploid cells

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a toy box.

**Haploid** is like having **one toy box** with half of your favorite toys inside.

**Diploid** is like having **two toy boxes**, each with half of your favorite toys. When you put them together, you have all your toys!

So, **haploid** cells have one set of toys (one set of chromosomes), and **diploid** cells have two sets of toys (two sets of chromosomes). 

In your body, most of your cells are diploid—they have two sets of toys! But when you make a baby, the egg and sperm are haploid—they each have just one set of toys. When they join, they make a new cell with two sets of toys again!
